terms.definition: A 2x2 portfolio planning framework created by Bruce Henderson (Boston Consulting Group, 1970). Maps strategic business units (SBUs) based on Relative Market Share (horizontal axis) and Market Growth Rate (vertical axis).
terms.formula: Relative Market Share = SBU Share / Leading Competitor Share

terms.definition: A firm's revenue or volume divided by that of its largest competitor. Plotted on a logarithmic scale. An RMS > 1.0 indicates market leadership and cost advantages from the Experience Curve.
High market share in a rapidly growing industry. Generate substantial cash but require heavy capital reinvestment (dark stores, marketing) to maintain market leadership.
terms.prescription: Build & Defend: Reinvest gross profit to scale capacity.

terms.definition: High market share in a mature, low-growth industry. Generate surplus cash flows with minimal capex requirements, which can cross-subsidize other business units.
terms.prescription: Hold & Harvest: Defend profitability and milk margins.

terms.definition: Low relative market share in a high-growth market. Consume large cash reserves while generating low returns. Face a strategic dilemma: either invest aggressively to become a Star or divest.
terms.prescription: Build or Divest: Double down on capital or exit.

terms.definition: Low relative market share in a mature or stagnant market. Often cash neutral or cash draining with limited growth upside.
terms.prescription: Harvest or Divest: Restructure, niche down, or liquidate.

terms.definition: A structural framework devised by Michael E. Porter (1979) identifying the five market forces that determine long-run industry profitability: Rivalry, Entrants, Substitutes, Buyer Power, Supplier Power.

A composite metric on a [0, 10] scale inversely related to weighted force hostility. 10 indicates a benign, monopolistically profitable industry; 0 indicates a hyper-competitive, margin-compressing squeeze.
An oligopoly model where firms compete simultaneously by setting prices. When products are close substitutes, price cuts trigger aggressive retaliation, driving prices down toward marginal cost.
A state in game theory (John Nash, 1950) where no player can unilaterally deviate from their chosen strategy to increase their own payoff, given the strategies chosen by competitors.
An administrative acronym coined by Luther Gulick and Lyndall Urwick (1937) outlining the executive functions: Planning, Organizing, Staffing, Directing, Coordinating, Reporting, and Budgeting.
terms.pomeUnit: Unit I: Evolution of Management Thought

terms.definition: The number of direct subordinates a manager supervises. A narrow span yields tall hierarchies (many layers, high coordination overhead); a wide span yields flat, agile organizations.
A measure of consumer responsiveness: percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price. If |Ed| > 1, demand is elastic; if |Ed| < 1, demand is inelastic.
